How iMiracle reads cell-to-cell signalling, one idea at a time

A cell’s genes respond to its own type and to the signals its neighbours send through ligand–receptor (LR) pairs. iMiracle separates the two, builds one communication graph per LR pair, and fills in the graphs that sparse data hide. The toy tissue below has two cell types and four LR pairs; boxes marked Paper quote the paper.

A cell’s expression: a cell-type baseline plus one term per LR pair

X = Xb + Σlr Xslr,   Xb = MLP(T),   ψ(lr, c, g) = Xslr[c, g]

The baseline depends only on the cell’s type. Each LR term depends on what that pair’s graph delivers to the cell, so two cells of the same type can differ. The toy gene g was built this way; color the tissue by its parts and tap a cell to split it.

LR pairs ranked by ψ for this cell and gene

    Paper In simulations with a known answer, iMiracle recovers best which LR pairs drive each gene in each cell. On human DLPFC, the top pairs for the gene GJA1 change from region to region, and two of its top three pairs were found only through iterative learning (Fig. 3, Sec. 4.3; Fig. 4E and 4I).

    Toy: 276 cells; the gene’s baseline is 1.1 in type A and 0.25 in type B, and each LR term is 0.055 × what the cell receives on that pair’s graph. Dashed circles are the zones where each pair signals strongly. In iMiracle the baseline and the terms are learned; here they are the toy’s ground truth.

    Keep an LR pair only if enough cells express it, then give it its own graph

    LRθ = { lr : ξl > θ and ξr > θ },   Glr[s → c] = El[s] · Er[c] / d(s, c)

    ξ is the fraction of cells in which the ligand (or receptor) is detected. Each kept pair gets its own weighted graph over the same cells: a sender’s ligand times the receiver’s receptor, divided by their distance, on each cell’s 5 nearest neighbours. Move θ, pick a pair, tap a cell.

    Paper Candidate pairs come from CellChatDB (3,267 human, 3,387 mouse pairs); θ = 15% and k = 5 neighbours by default. Each kept pair’s graph goes through its own GNN; a shared decoder maps the embeddings to expression, optionally masked by a gene regulatory or protein interaction network (Sec. 3.2).

    Toy: counts after random dropout (about 40% of non-zero entries kept), as spatial data look before imputation.

    Impute, re-check, add the pairs that now pass, repeat

    Glr(i+1) = α Glr(i) + (1 − α) Glr(X(i)) for pairs already in;  new pairs start from Glr(X(i))

    Dropouts hide ligands and receptors, so some real pairs fail θ at first. After training, the imputed matrix X is checked again: pairs that now pass join the graph, and the graphs already in are refreshed with a blend of old and new. Training stops when no pair is added.

      rebuilt from X onlykeep the old graph

      Paper On real data, iterative learning adds 27 to 56 LR pairs per 10x Visium sample (up to 181% more), 16 on Stereo-seq and 26 on Slide-seqV2. α = 0.2 works best; at α = 0 the graphs follow only the newest imputation, at α = 1 they never change, and both lose precision (Fig. 2A, Fig. 6A). Imputation error on Slide-seqV2: 0.407 RMSE, against 0.765 for STAGATE (Table 3).

      Toy: the “imputed” matrix is the toy’s counts before dropout, which is what imputation aims to recover; iMiracle gets there by training.

      Toys, not results: a small simulated tissue built like the paper’s simulation (Sec. 3.4) and computed with its formulas (Eqs. 1–2 and 6–13). iMiracle: Duan et al., CIKM 2024.
